answer.why: As an insider, 'Confirmed & Substantive' made me laugh immediately: it is the exact phrase you wait years to see on your appointment, and it tells me the designers know how the service really talks. 'Minister Salary' is the cheap headline everyone in Singapore has opinions about, so it feels like bait. I'd tap the quieter name because it suggests they got the details right, though a stranger scrolling past might have no idea what it means.
answer.expect_minister_salary: A satirical or political game about ministerial pay, probably with a punchy, slightly cynical tone. I'd expect it to focus on the benchmarking debate and the climb to the top, and I'd worry it would get the details wrong, flatten the service into a get-rich-as-a-minister joke, and ignore the daily grind of policy work.
answer.expect_confirmed_substantive: A dry, insider-flavoured sim about the unglamorous reality of a civil service career: probation, confirmation, appointments, grades, appraisals and waiting for the paperwork to catch up with the work. I'd expect gentle humour about bureaucracy and more accurate detail, though it might feel obscure or boring to anyone outside the service.

worst_moment.what: The Cabinet question on indicators cost me 14 STAND with no explanation, then a single-option townhall workload question I could only answer. It felt like being punished with no say.

skip_year.why: Another townhall question with only one option. I tapped through it, and the STAND slide just carried on without any new decision.

callbacks_noticed.earlier_choice: Nominated the quiet officer for PSLP
callbacks_noticed.came_back_as: She later backed me, and the ending shows the choice raised my ceiling to DPM

callbacks_noticed.earlier_choice: Answered the workload question honestly at townhalls
callbacks_noticed.came_back_as: The same workload and hybrid work questions returned in Y34 and Y35 with only one option

callbacks_noticed.earlier_choice: Asked in Cabinet whether ministers should be paid on indicators they set
callbacks_noticed.came_back_as: A STAND drop of 14, though appraisals stayed outstanding

answer.held_back_by: Probably my own habit of asking awkward questions in rooms where people prefer a tidy answer. Being right about the indicators cost me standing. Still, I got to PM, so nothing held me back much.
answer.ending_fair_why: Clean integrity and a published formula fit the career I played. The DECLASSIFIED card was the best part because it showed what my choices did. I never saw the pilot, the kueh man, the quoting MP or the board offer pay off, which was a letdown.
answer.chase_next: I would try the path where the party's estimate gets overridden early, or a run that takes the conglomerate board seat. I want to see whether leaving the service shows me a different ceiling.
answer.play_again_why: It was a good run, but I'm fairly sure I've seen the shape of it. I'd come back on another commute, not straight away.

tone_breaks.line: You made it. The formula pays you twice the entry-grade minister's salary, and the formula was published, so nobody can say they were not told.
tone_breaks.note: A pointed line about the real benchmark. It reads as the game commenting on itself rather than the world. The 'twice entry-grade' figure also looks oversimplified for a PM.

tone_breaks.line: Your file is clean enough to be boring. In this building, that is a compliment.
tone_breaks.note: Funny, and insiders would laugh, but it is the game nudging the player.

answer.title_fit_why: What stuck with me was the appraisal and ceiling machinery, not the pay. The salary was a number on a card, but being confirmed and substantive in a grade is what the game was really about.
